paras: The Smyrna riot was an armed clash near midnight on 1 August 1895 near Smyrna, Cobb County, Georgia, in which a white posse hunting Jesse Hardeman, a Black farm hand accused of attempting to assault a white woman, stopped and fired on his father, his brother and two other Black men. Three of the Black men were shot, a fourth was missing afterward, and a white man, Charley Dowda, was wounded in the hand. Wire reports called it a "pitched battle" and warned of a Black "uprising"; sworn testimony split over who fired first.

According to the Marietta Journal, Hardeman, a tenant on Polly Baswell's farm, was accused of seizing Mrs. Joe Robinson, a fellow tenant's wife, at her house on Tuesday, 30 July (the wire said Saturday); she drove him off with a pistol and he escaped to the woods. A warrant was issued and armed neighbors searched for him, and on 1 August a rumor spread in Smyrna that he had been hanged from Collins' bridge over the Chattahoochee at Bolton.

Hearing the rumor, John Hardeman, Jesse's father, set out armed for the bridge with his son Tom, Berry Padgett and Berry Smith, two in a cart and two on mules. By John Hardeman's account, they were heading home, satisfied the report was false, when three white men, among them Virgil Fleming, stopped them at pistol point and sent them on to a large armed crowd. The whites demanded that they account for themselves and give up their guns, Tom surrendered his, and shooting broke out as the Black men fled.

John Hardeman was shot through the left leg, Tom in the leg, and Padgett in the head, neck and shoulders with bird shot. Berry Smith was not seen again; the Constitution called him seriously wounded, and the Journal did not know whether he was alive. Dowda had sixty-five shot picked from his hand, and two mules were shot, one fatally.

At a hearing before Judge J. Y. Alexander in Marietta on 3 August, John Hardeman was committed for assault with intent to murder in default of a $500 bond, he and a William Hardeman were committed for riot, Padgett and Tom Hardeman gave bond, and Jacob Thomas, who had lent a mule, was discharged. The Marietta Rifles were alerted on the night of 2 August but, the Journal said, were not needed because "the matter was unduly magnified."

As of 7 August Jesse Hardeman was still at large, said to be hidden near Gilmore station with a large posse after him. The coverage does not show his capture, any grand jury action, or Berry Smith's fate.

The first Atlanta dispatch, of 2 August, described "a pitched battle" with five or six Black men "all fully armed," said one fired first from a wagon, misnamed the wounded white man "Charles Boughly," and warned that "a great uprising of the negroes is imminent." Papers from Santa Fe to Raleigh ran it on 2 and 3 August under headlines such as "Race War in Georgia," "A War of Races Imminent" and "Hunting for a Rapist," the last with the deck "A Justly Indignant Party."

A second dispatch, in Savannah and Birmingham, still said Jesse's father "started the shooting." The Atlanta Constitution's Marietta correspondent then printed the Hardemans' statement that the whites fired first, noting that no white participant had given one; its hearing report ran in Savannah and Birmingham on 4 August. The Marietta Journal's account on 8 August, headed "A Negro Assaults a White Woman," called the searchers "Indignant Citizens" and adopted the posse's version, but printed the Black defendants' testimony beside it.

John Hardeman said the white men began shooting after ordering them to throw up their hands, and that he fired once only after the crowd opened fire; Tom Hardeman testified that "Dowda shot first." Posse members W. A. Gaston and Virgil Fleming swore instead that John Hardeman jumped from the cart, fired at Dowda and told the others to shoot. The Journal also reported, as hearsay, that the party was "bent on preventing the lynching," whereas John Hardeman said they had only gone to see whether Jesse had been hanged.

reader.title: Smyrna riot (1895)
bases: An armed white posse of twenty or thirty men hunting an accused Black man stopped four of his relatives and friends on the road and a shooting followed in which three or four Black men and one white man were wounded and no death was confirmed (A11, A14, A15).

The Atlanta wire (A1, A4), an Atlanta Constitution special (A11) and the local Marietta Journal (A14, A15) independently report the clash, its participants and wounded, though they disagree on who fired first.

accounts.label: First Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: A posse of about twenty hunting Jesse Hardeman met five or six fully armed Black men; one rose in a wagon and fired both barrels of a shotgun, and the whites returned about a hundred shots.

accounts.label: Second Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: The posse met Hardeman's father, brother and friends, who had heard he had been lynched; the father started the shooting; four Black men and one white man were seriously wounded.

accounts.label: John and Tom Hardeman (Black participants)
accounts.gist: Returning home from near the Bolton bridge, they were stopped at pistol point, made to give up a gun and throw up their hands, and then the white men began shooting, Dowda first; John fired once and ran only after the crowd fired.

accounts.label: Berry Padgett (Black participant)
accounts.gist: Questioned by the crowd, he saw John jump from the cart and was then shot from behind as his mule bolted; he had no gun.

accounts.label: Posse members' testimony
accounts.gist: Gaston and Virgil Fleming swore John Hardeman jumped from the cart, fired at Dowda and told the others to shoot; Bob Fleming said Tom Hardeman snapped a gun at Norris Pace.

accounts.label: Marietta Journal narrative
accounts.gist: The Black men were said to be 'bent on preventing the lynching'; when asked to account for themselves and surrender their guns, John Hardeman fired at Dowda and a fusillade followed.

framing.detail: The national wire called the searchers 'friends and relatives of the woman', had the Black party fire first, called Hardeman 'the fiend' and warned 'a great uprising of the negroes is imminent', under heads like 'Race War in Georgia' and 'A War of Races Imminent'.
The Raleigh News and Observer headed the wire 'Hunting for a Rapist' with decks 'A Justly Indignant Party' and 'The Battle Begun by the Negroes'.

The Atlanta Constitution special called it 'a serious riot', treated the alleged assault as fact, but printed the Hardemans' account that the whites fired first and noted no white statement had been obtained.

The Marietta Journal headed it 'A Negro Assaults a White Woman' and called the searchers 'Indignant Citizens', gave its own version that John Hardeman fired first, yet printed both sides' testimony and called the scare 'unduly magnified'.

versions.value: A Black man in a wagon fired both barrels at the approaching posse
John Hardeman fired at Dowda first and told the others to shoot (posse witnesses Gaston and V. Fleming; Marietta Journal narrative)
The whites disarmed them, ordered hands up and then fired, Dowda first (John and Tom Hardeman)

conflicts.note: Every version comes from one side; the sworn testimony at the Aug. 3 hearing split along racial lines, and the court committed John Hardeman.
The two Georgia local accounts agree on Tuesday and give circumstantial detail; the wire's Saturday is likely the error.

versions.value: Said to be 'bent on preventing the lynching'
Going to see if Jesse had been hanged at the bridge, and turning home once satisfied the report was false

conflicts.note: The Journal's version is hearsay ('It is said'); the second is John Hardeman's own statement.

versions.value: Charles Boughly / Boughtly / Doughty / Dougty, ninety buckshot in the left arm
Charley Dowda, shot in the left hand, sixty-five shot picked out

conflicts.note: The wire names appear to be garbles of Dowda; the local reports are better evidence.

versions.value: Seriously wounded; one Black man may have died
Not seen since; not known whether killed or wounded

conflicts.note: No later report of his fate was found.

record_check.dossier: The clash was near midnight on Thursday, 1 August 1895; 27 July is the wire's 'Saturday night last' date for the alleged assault, which the Georgia papers place on Tuesday, 30 July.
Near Smyrna, on the road between Smyrna and Bolton, Cobb County; Marietta was the site of the hearing.
Those fired on were John Hardeman, Tom Hardeman, Berry Padgett and Berry Smith; Jesse Hardeman was the accused, not present; 'Charles Boughly' is a wire garble of Charley Dowda, a white posse member.
3 confirmed (John Hardeman, Tom Hardeman, Padgett); 4 if Berry Smith, reported seriously wounded and missing, is counted.
1 named (Charley Dowda); the Constitution said other unnamed whites were also wounded.
Named posse members: Virgil Fleming (deputized), Norris Pace, Charley Dowda, W. A. Gaston; 20-30 men.

record_check.record: accused of attempting to assault the wife of J. H. Robinson
record_check.dossier: Jesse Hardeman was accused of attempting a criminal assault on Mrs. Joe Robinson; the men actually shot were his relatives and friends, accused of no prior offense (later charged with riot and assault with intent to murder).

record_check.record: posse fired on a party of Black men; Charles Boughly was hit by buckshot
record_check.dossier: The man hit by buckshot was white (Dowda); three or four of the Black party were wounded, and both sides gave opposite accounts of who fired first.
15 white-press articles in 11 papers, 2-8 August 1895; no Black-press coverage found.

info: Near midnight on Thursday night, 1 August 1895 ('last night' in a special dated Aug. 2; 'Thursday night'; 'night before last' in an Aug. 3 report)

On the public road about halfway between Smyrna and Bolton, near Mr. King's house, after the Black party turned back from near Collins' bridge over the Chattahoochee at Bolton; the wire placed it about two miles east, between Marietta and Atlanta
John Hardeman (Jesse's father, over 50), Tom Hardeman (Jesse's brother), Berry Padgett and Berry Smith, Black men stopped and fired on by the posse

Jesse Hardeman, a Black farm hand on the same farm, was accused of attempting a criminal assault on Mrs. Joe Robinson, a white woman, at her house late on a Tuesday (30 July); the first wire said 'Saturday night last'

A posse of white neighbors and searchers, among them Virgil Fleming (who testified he had been deputized to hunt Jesse Hardeman), Norris Pace, Charley Dowda and W. A. Gaston; the wire said Sheriff Davenport organized a large posse
None confirmed; the Constitution said one Black man 'it is thought, may have died', and Berry Smith had not been seen since, his fate unknown
Jesse Hardeman had not been arrested as of the Aug. 7 report and was said to be hidden near Gilmore station; no report of his capture or of any trial was found
